lead: A compass turns direction into a number from the earth's magnetic field, so the number is only as good as the field at that spot. Iron objects, steel tapes, phones and cables carrying current bend the needle; bearings still look reasonable while wrong. This chapter reads a bearing, builds the two checks that expose a bent needle, finds clean stations and corrects the rest.
prereq: You need: Chapter 2.1 for whole circle bearings, back bearings and interior angles, and Unit 1 for angular units, error and precision.

sections.h3: The compass, its least count and its adjustments

blocks.text: A compass needle is a small magnet on a sharp pivot. It swings until it lies along the magnetic meridian, and a graduated ring shows how far the line of sight is from that meridian. Read the ring and you have the magnetic bearing of the line.

The plain (surveyor's) compass fixes the ring to the box and moves the needle inside it; you read quadrantal bearings, 0° to 90°. The prismatic compass carries the ring on the needle and puts a prism at the eye, so graduations and object are seen together. It reads whole circle bearings, 0° to 360° clockwise from magnetic north, with least count 30′ (half a degree), the smallest change the ring can show.
Temporary adjustments, repeated at every station:

items: Fix the compass on its tripod and centre it over the station with a plumb bob.
Level the box, so the needle swings freely.
Release the needle, let it settle, and tap the glass to overcome friction.
Adjust the prism until graduations are sharp and the ranging rod is bisected by the sighting hair.
Let the needle rest, read the ring, and book the station, line, and fore or back bearing.

sections.h3: Compass traverse and its two checks

blocks.text: A compass traverse measures the bearing of each line in turn. In a closed traverse the last station is the first, as round a plot boundary. In an open traverse the line ends at a point not yet fixed, as along a road centre line; it has no closing check, so tie it to known points.

At each station read two bearings: the fore bearing (FB) of the line ahead, and the back bearing (BB) of the line behind. Both describe the same line from opposite ends, so they must differ by half a circle.

blocks.where: FB is the fore bearing at the station, in degrees clockwise from magnetic north; BB is the back bearing of the same line at the far station; use + when BB < 180° (answer stays below 360°) and − when BB > 180°. A difference other than 180° means local attraction at one of the two stations.

blocks.text: The second check works only on a closed polygon and uses the interior angles.

blocks.where: n is the number of sides of the closed polygon and the sum is in degrees: 180° for a triangle, 360° for a quadrilateral, 540° for a pentagon.

blocks.text: An interior angle at a station comes from the two bearings there: take their difference, and choose the value inside the polygon. If the measured sum is S, the angular error is e = S − (2n − 4) × 90°. Correct every angle by −e/n, and put any leftover minute on the angle between the two shortest lines.

The needle obeys every magnetic field, not only the earth's. A steel tape, an iron railing, a truck, iron ore, a key, or a cable carrying current adds its own field. The needle then points somewhere other than magnetic north. Every bearing at that station is turned by the same small angle, from a few minutes to a few degrees, and the next clean station reads normally.

Detection is a test on a line, not on one station. If the fore and back bearings of a line differ by exactly 180°, both its stations are free from local attraction. Start from such a line and walk through the traverse; the first station you cannot vouch for is the one to correct.

Method 1, interior angles. Compute the interior angle at every station from the observed bearings, check the sum against (2n − 4) × 90°, share the error, then work out corrected bearings outward from a line known to be true. Local attraction cancels in the angles because it enters both bearings at a station by the same amount.

Method 2, direct from an unaffected line. Take the correct bearing of a line at a free station, add or subtract 180° for its correct back bearing, and compare that with the observed back bearing at the far station. The difference is the correction at that station. Apply it to every bearing taken there, move to the next line, and repeat. The corrections must still agree when you return to the start.

items: Needle not free: a blunt pivot or grit makes it stick; tap the glass and see if it returns to the same reading.
Compass not level: a tilted needle rubs and drags; level the box each time.
Sighting: the ranging rod must stand vertical and be bisected by the hair; read the ring square through the prism.
Magnetic declination: the angle between true north and magnetic north changes with place and slowly with time, so note the date and place of the survey; defined in Chapter 2.1.
Keep tapes, keys, phones, iron pegs and magnets away from the compass, never stand over it with a steel chain, and always book both fore and back bearings.

spec.title: Interior angle method
spec.aria: A flow chart of the interior angle method: observed bearings give interior angles, the angle sum is checked, the error is shared, and corrected bearings are computed and back-checked.

examples.question: The observed bearings of a closed compass traverse ABCD are: AB 46°00′, BA 226°00′, BC 130°00′, CB 310°00′, CD 220°30′, DC 40°00′, DA 309°30′, AD 130°00′. Find the stations free from local attraction, the correction at each affected station, and all corrected bearings.
steps: Test each line. AB − BA = 46°00′ − 226°00′ = −180°00′; magnitude exactly 180°, so A and B are free.
BC − CB = 130°00′ − 310°00′ = −180°00′; B is free, so BC = 130°00′ is correct and correct CB = 310°00′, equal to observed CB. Station C is free.
C is free, so CD = 220°30′ stands. Correct DC = 220°30′ − 180°00′ = 40°30′. Observed DC is 40°00′, so D reads 30′ too small: correction at D = +30′.
Apply +30′ at D: DC = 40°30′, DA = 310°00′. Check: correct AD at A = 310°00′ − 180°00′ = 130°00′, equal to observed AD. The loop closes.
Interior angles from corrected bearings: A = AD − AB = 84°00′; B = BA − BC = 96°00′; C = CB − CD = 89°30′; D = (DC + 360°00′) − DA = 40°30′ + 360°00′ − 310°00′ = 90°30′.
examples.answer: Stations A, B and C are free; D carries +30′. Corrected bearings: AB 46°00′, BA 226°00′, BC 130°00′, CB 310°00′, CD 220°30′, DC 40°30′, DA 310°00′, AD 130°00′; interior angles 84°00′, 96°00′, 89°30′, 90°30′ sum to 360°00′.
examples.check:
fb = {'AB': 46.0, 'BC': 130.0, 'CD': 220.5, 'DA': 309.5}
bb = {'BA': 226.0, 'CB': 310.0, 'DC': 40.0, 'AD': 130.0}
corr = {'A': 0.0, 'B': 0.0, 'C': 0.0, 'D': 0.0}
corr['D'] = (fb['CD'] - 180.0) - bb['DC']
print(round(corr['D'] * 60.0, 1))
AB = fb['AB'] + corr['A']
AD = bb['AD'] + corr['A']
BC = fb['BC'] + corr['B']
CB = bb['CB'] + corr['B']
CD = fb['CD'] + corr['C']
DC = bb['DC'] + corr['D']
DA = fb['DA'] + corr['D']
A = AD - AB
B = bb['BA'] - BC
C = CB - CD
D = (DC + 360.0) - DA
print(A)
print(B)
print(C)
print(D)
print(A + B + C + D)

traps: Taking the first station as free. Only a line whose fore and back bearings differ by 180° proves two stations free.
Applying a station correction to bearings taken elsewhere. A correction belongs to the station where the needle was read.
Sign slip in FB = BB ± 180°: add when BB < 180°, subtract when BB > 180°.
Mixing local attraction with magnetic declination. Declination is between true and magnetic north; local attraction changes station to station.
Reporting the exterior angle when the interior was asked. If the bearing difference exceeds 180°, the interior angle is 360° minus that difference.

quiz.q: What is the least count of a prismatic compass, and what does it mean?
quiz.a: 30′, half a degree; the smallest change in bearing the ring can show.

quiz.q: State the two arithmetic checks used in a compass traverse.
quiz.a: For every line, the fore and back bearings differ by 180° (magnitude); for a closed polygon of n sides, sum of interior angles = (2n − 4) × 90°.

quiz.q: Why does local attraction cancel out of an interior angle?
quiz.a: Both bearings at that station turn by the same angle, so their difference is unchanged. The angle stays right while the bearings are wrong.

quiz.q: At station P the bearing of PQ is 120°00′ and of PR is 250°00′. Find the angle QPR.
quiz.a: 250°00′ − 120°00′ = 130°00′. This is the smaller angle between the two directions and is under 180°, so it is taken as it stands; if the difference had exceeded 180°, the angle would be 360° minus that difference.

quiz.q: A closed traverse has 6 sides. What should its interior angles sum to?
The interior angles of a closed quadrilateral measure 84°00′, 96°00′, 89°30′ and 91°00′. How much error is there and how is it shared?
quiz.a: Sum = 360°30′ against 360°00′, so e = +30′; correction per angle = −30′/4 = −7′30″.

quiz.q: In a traverse ABCD the fore and back bearings of AB differ by exactly 180°, but those of CD differ by 179°30′. Which stations can you trust, and what is your next step?
quiz.a: A and B are free. Take BC as correct from B, compute correct CB, compare with observed CB for the correction at C, then carry on to D. The CD pair shows whether C or D caused the 30′.

beyond: Not for the exam. A total station computes bearings from coordinates without a needle, and GNSS gives true azimuth directly, so the compass is no longer the main direction instrument. It survives in reconnaissance, underground and forest work, and in checking that a site is magnetically quiet before a magnetic survey. Phone magnetometers and geomagnetic models estimate magnetic north anywhere. Search for 'magnetic declination calculator' and 'magnetometer survey' to go further.
